title: End of Debate - AI is another tool to use
author: Any_Inevitable_4035
selftext:
Every new tool got the same “that’s cheating” reaction: photography was supposed to kill painting, synths were supposed to kill “real” musicians, Photoshop was supposed to kill skill. Each time, the tool became normal and people found new ways to be creative with it. AI fits that pattern in a lot of ways.

There’s one real difference, though. Earlier tools mostly extended your hands: a camera captures what you point it at, and a brush does what you move it to do. AI can make creative decisions itself, like composition, wording, melody, or style. So the open question is how much of the result came from you.

Here’s a practical way to think about it. If you’re steering, choosing, editing, and putting your own taste and intent into it, AI works like any other tool. If you type a prompt and accept whatever comes out, it’s closer to commissioning someone else than to using a tool.

There’s also the training-data debate. Older tools weren’t built from other artists’ work, so artists’ concerns about consent and credit are a fair point, and they’re separate from the “is it a tool” question.

So it’s a tool, but a more powerful one, and that makes how you use it matter more.

replies.author: throwaway098242
replies.body:
A: Maybe, but not without significant research breakthroughs. It's not like it's guaranteed to be impossible, we just don't know. It depends on what intelligence or will is, and how hard it is to achieve it.

AI progress is very "spiky", there are monumental discoveries (the "Attention is all you need"-paper), followed by periods of relatively dry, simple improvements of tooling, training optimizations, architecture optimizations etc. Before LLMs, we had CNNs, the invention of RELU, Resnets, word2vec, LSTMs and so on. Not in chronological order, just kinda listing what comes to mind. It's a long chain of milestones in mathematical foundations and discoveries of new network architectures.

It's not really possible to predict the next big thing, and it could even plateau at some point. I mean, it's easy to assume it's just gonna keep improving, but you would expect this for every scientific field, and yet we've been pretty much hardstuck in physics for a few decades now. Quantum mechanics and special relativity were both discovered at basically the same time around 1900-ish, but these two fuckers still contradict each other till today, and we don't know how to resolve that.

replies.author: Flashy-Presence-2467
replies.body:
I think you guys are almost making a category error by asking "will it get better."

The reason AI has no initial will isn't necessarily because it cannot, it's because those aren't profitable or safe uses. Most of the models we have came out of chat-based, purely responsive LLMs, and have only recently added *some* agentic capabilities. The lobotomized, corporate sort of AI experience you are having where it executes and reflects your own ideas is intentional and the result of alignment training.

I don't think that we want fully autonomous agents that are capable of making their own decisions and acting upon the world. Even if they are only similar to our own intelligence and not vastly higher, that is not a world that we continue to own.

It is actually quite critical that we do not allow development of AI agent swarms that have their own goals. Those AI's are not "better" they are just more persistent and contradictory to humanity's own goals.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
Yes; it's just a statistical model. It only seems smart because it is working in an area that humans are horrible at working in. 

Current technology does raise a lot of questions about the nature of intelligence that we should take seriously, but there's no evidence right now that LLMs are doing anything other than rolling down statistical hills. If humans had a better intuition of statistics, nothing they do would look like intelligence.

comments.author: PoisonSD
comments.body:
It's not just a tool if it's like commissioning someone else. Using a tool is 100% your own work still, if it's like commissioning someone else it's no longer 100% your own work. I feel mostly this way towards art made with AI, it's not just a tool if you're only "ordering" a piece of art from it. 

 With code I feel different, because of how close I am to the resulting architecture, it needs to go through tons of iterations and I can look and make decisions about how I want something to perform. Suggest actual solutions and see them created. 

It's a tool when it comes to code, and with art its a contractor, because telling it what to do has very little direct impact on the resulting artwork.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
The similarities with photography are downright eerie. 

It's literally all of the same arguments, right down to photographs being seen as slop because the photographic technology was in its infancy and also because people were so used to portrait paintings and lithographs that photographs looked uncanny and unflattering by comparison. A camera is going to catch blemishes and imperfections that a portrait artist would leave out.   
  
Cameras could not, allegedly, capture the 'majesty' of a thing, because photography couldn't lie to the audience (I mean, it totally could, but not in the same way).   
  
Portrait artists and lithographers were scared they'd go out of work... and they were not wrong. But the economy is not supposed to have protected classes of people in it.   
  
  
Literally 100 years passed before photography was finally accepted as an art form. Perhaps most tellingly, this happened in the New World first - and that's where the modern film studios and animation studios ended up. Europe fell behind culturally.   


I have this suspicion we're watching the same thing happen right now, just in fast forward mode. Western culture isn't accepting AI, but the Global South is. So that's where the action will happen. Anyone in North America will be left behind.   


...It's kind of hilarious and depressing how obvious this is when using local models. If I have MOSS generate images of people, all of them are always aesthetically Asian. That's the new cultural default as far as the models are concerned, because that's who's embracing the technology. :|

Ok, and what about the environmental debate?  The economic debate?  The philosophical value of human works debate?  The conglomeration of power into the hands of a few debate?  The saturation of the domain debate?  The fairness of the sources of training data debate?

I understand that everyone is going to have their own takes on AI, but this is just "it works for me, so I'm not going to think about it past that".

It's not "***just*** a tool".  It's a service built on a mountain of infrastructure that has wide-reaching implications.
